title: Volunteer's Folly
hook: Free help can be costly when the helper is pulled from work only they can do.
counterintuition: Volunteering is not automatically noble use of time. The real question is comparative advantage: who can create the most value in each role, including the work displaced by the favor?
tryThisNow: Before offering help today, write the task, your best alternative use of that hour, and who could do the task well at lower opportunity cost.
keyTakeaway: Do not price help at zero; price it by the value of the work it displaces.

breakdown.fastRead:
The parking ticket on Carys's hospital triage desk belongs to the surgeon who spent an hour moving supply boxes because volunteers were short. The boxes got moved. Two consults waited. Carys marks volunteer folly on the ticket and calls facilities for the next shift.

Volunteer's folly appears when free labor hides its opportunity cost. A skilled person can do a simple task, but that does not make it the best use of them. The cost is the work that did not happen while they helped.

A free hour is not free if it came from the wrong person.
breakdown.deepRead:
The parking ticket makes the choice visible. The surgeon was generous. Nobody should sneer at that. But generosity does not erase comparative advantage. If a porter can move boxes safely and a surgeon can clear consults that no porter can clear, the hospital loses value when the surgeon becomes the porter.

This is not an argument against service. It is an argument for putting service where it helps most. You may feel virtuous doing a task by hand because your time feels donated. But the world still pays the opportunity cost. A lawyer who spends Saturday sorting donated clothes may create less value than by funding two trained sorters and taking one urgent legal-aid case. A manager who fixes every spreadsheet may rob the team of the decision only she can make.

Good intent does not cancel tradeoffs.

Verena sees this in a seafood export cold-storage bid. A safety glove lies beside a freezer repair quote after the owner says his cousin can install the panels for free. Verena marks comparative advantage on the glove and compares the cousin's weekend labor with spoilage risk, warranty loss, and the owner's missed buyer calls.

The correction is to ask where each person has the strongest advantage. Who can do this task well? What else would they otherwise do? What fails if they are busy here? Sometimes the answer is still volunteer. Sometimes the answer is pay the specialist, donate money, or step aside.
breakdown.fullRead:
The ticket stub on Elsa's port scheduling desk is from a charity gala where the harbor director promised staff would build birdhouses for a shoreline fundraiser. The carpenters are booked on berth repairs. The planners are behind on tide windows. The birdhouses would be charming, but Elsa marks birdhouses on the stub and asks what the fundraiser gains compared with what the port loses.

Comparative advantage is usually linked to David Ricardo: even if one person or country is better at two tasks, it can still make sense to specialize where the relative advantage is strongest and trade for the rest. The idea feels cold until you see what it protects. It protects scarce skill from being spent where another person can do the work almost as well while the skilled person does what only they can do.

What is the hidden work displaced by your good deed?

A birdhouse example makes the point plain. If a highly paid professional spends a day making rough birdhouses for a charity sale, the visible labor looks generous. But if a carpenter or factory can make better birdhouses cheaply, the professional may create more value by doing their best work for a day and donating the earnings. A reader once pointed out that manufacturing the birdhouses where they can be made efficiently may beat both the professional and the local carpenter. The moral is not local versus foreign. The moral is advantage and opportunity cost.

You face the same issue in a fintech model review. You are beside Ruben, holding a thermometer from an overheated server room while the lead data scientist offers to spend Friday labeling support tickets. The tickets matter. The model audit also matters, and only she can finish it before a compliance deadline. Ruben marks opportunity cost on the thermometer and hires temporary labelers.

Volunteer's folly gets emotional because the visible helper looks admirable and the absent work is invisible. Nobody applauds the consult that would have been cleared, the buyer call that would have saved a shipment, or the model check that prevented a fine. The room sees the boxes moved. The hidden loss needs someone to name it.

Eve learns that in a school literacy intervention. A price card shows a reading specialist has been photocopying take-home packets because the office is short-staffed. The packets are useful. The missed small-group lessons are more valuable. Eve marks Ricardo on the price card and moves packet prep to a paid aide while the specialist returns to decoding sessions.

Niklas sees the postmortem version in a limited bakery batch. A trial binder shows the pastry chef spent two mornings designing free charity signage instead of testing oven times for a seasonal loaf. The signage was kind. The loaf failed at scale. Niklas marks volunteer on the binder and changes the next charity plan: donate a fixed amount from sales and keep the chef on the work only she can do.

Do not price help at zero; price it by the value of the work it displaces.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Volunteer's Folly helps readers see opportunity cost inside generous offers. The goal is better allocation of skill, not less generosity.

reviewCards.front: A skilled person offers free help. What cost should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the opportunity cost: what work only that person can do, and what disappears while they do the simple task.

reviewCards.front: How does comparative advantage change volunteering?
reviewCards.back: It asks where each person creates the most relative value. The best help may be money, delegation, or specialist work instead of direct labor.

reviewCards.front: Why can handmade charity work be wasteful?
reviewCards.back: If someone else can make the item better or cheaper, the volunteer may create more value by doing their own high-advantage work and funding the item.

reviewCards.front: What makes volunteer folly emotionally hard to spot?
reviewCards.back: The visible helper looks generous, while the displaced work is invisible. You have to name the hidden loss.

reviewCards.front: What is the right attitude toward the helper?
reviewCards.back: Thank the intention, then reassign the task by advantage. The point is better use of generosity, not shaming service.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Price free help by opportunity cost. Before accepting or offering a task, ask who has the strongest advantage and what higher-value work would be displaced.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I offer to help with a simple task, then I will first name the work only I can do during that same hour.
If a skilled person fills a gap, then I will compare that fix with hiring, delegating, or simplifying the task.
If handmade labor feels virtuous, then I will compare it with buying the item and donating the saved high-value time.
If I keep doing a task because I am good at it, then I will ask whether someone else can do it well enough while I handle the decision only I can make.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one act of help, write the task, your displaced work, and the person or service with lower opportunity cost.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a generous task you performed. Ask whether the same generosity would have created more value through delegation, payment, or specialist work.
